# Systemic lupus erythematosus

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Rheumatology and immunology > Connective tissue diseases > Systemic lupus erythematosus*

[Original Article Link](/library/dT0op2)

---

## Summary

Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a multisystem autoimmune disease that predominantly affects women of childbearing age and is the most common form of lupus. The exact cause is still unknown, but hormonal and immunological features and genetic predisposition are considered likely etiological factors. Disease presentation is variable but is usually characterized by phases of remission and relapse. Symptoms can range from mild and localized to life-threatening systemic disease. SLE can affect any organ, but typical findings include <u>arthritis</u>, a <u>malar rash</u> (facial <u>butterfly rash</u>), and <u>constitutional symptoms</u> such as <u>fever</u> and fatigue. Involvement of the <u>kidneys</u> is common and can lead to <u>lupus nephritis</u>. Potential manifestations of SLE include <u>cutaneous lupus erythematosus</u> (CLE) and <u>neuropsychiatric systemic lupus erythematosus</u> (<u>NPSLE</u>); however, they can also occur independently from SLE. Other forms of lupus in addition to SLE include <u>drug-induced lupus erythematosus</u> (<u>DILE</u>) and <u>neonatal lupus</u>. The diagnosis of lupus is based on clinical findings and is further supported by <u>laboratory studies</u>, including the presence of <u>antinuclear antibodies</u> (<u>ANAs</u>) and <u>antigen-specific ANAs</u> (i.e., <u>anti-dsDNA</u>, <u>anti-Sm</u>). The <u>2019 EULAR/ACR classification criteria for SLE</u> do not need to be fulfilled to make a diagnosis but may further support it. Management consists of general measures, such as avoiding sun exposure, and <u>lifestyle modifications for ASCVD prevention</u>. Long-term <u>immunosuppressive therapy</u> depends on disease severity and organ involvement; <u>hydroxychloroquine</u> is typically used, as it has been shown to reduce flares and decrease mortality. In severe cases, additional <u>immunosuppressants</u> (e.g., <u>mycophenolate</u>, <u>azathioprine</u>) or <u>biological agents</u> may be given. Cardiovascular, neurological, and renal disease (<u>lupus nephritis</u>), together with infections, are the main <u>causes of death</u> in patients with SLE.

## Epidemiology

* Sex: : <u>♀</u> > <u>♂</u> (10:1) [[1]](/library/GMbBJ8)

* Peak <u>incidence</u> and <u>prevalence</u> [[1]](/library/GMbBJ8)[[2]](/library/sMbtJ8)

* Age of onset

* Women: 15–44 years

* Men: no particular age

* Race: highest in populations of African descent




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Etiology

The exact etiology is unknown, but several predisposing factors have been identified.




* Genetic predisposition [[3]](/library/HMbKJ8)

* <u>HLA-DR2</u> and <u>HLA-DR3</u> are commonly present in individuals with SLE.

* Genetic deficiency of <u>classical pathway</u> <u>complement proteins</u> (<u>C1q</u>, C2, C4) in approx. 10% of affected individuals

* Hormonal factors: <u>Hyperestrogenic</u> states (e.g., due to <u>oral contraceptive</u> use, <u>postmenopausal</u> hormonal therapy, <u>endometriosis</u>) are associated with an increased risk of SLE. [[4]](/library/bLYHwp)

* Environmental factors [[3]](/library/HMbKJ8)[[4]](/library/bLYHwp)

* <u>Cigarette smoking</u> and silica exposure increase the risk of developing SLE.

* <u>UV light</u> and <u>EBV infection</u> may trigger disease flares, but there is insufficient evidence on whether they cause SLE.

* Drugs such as <u>procainamide</u> or <u>hydralazine</u> (see “<u>Drug-induced lupus erythematosus</u>”)

---

## Pathophysiology

The exact pathomechanism of SLE is not fully understood, but the following two processes are the most widely accepted hypotheses: [[5]](/library/RKYlTJ)




* <u>Autoantibody</u> development: deficiency of classical <u>complement proteins</u> (<u>C1q</u>, C4, C2) → failure of <u>macrophages</u> to <u>phagocytose</u> <u>immune complexes</u> and <u>apoptotic</u> cell material (i.e., plasma and nuclear <u>antigens</u>) → dysregulated, intolerant <u>lymphocytes</u> targeting normally hidden intracellular <u>antigens</u> → <u>autoantibody</u> production (e.g., <u>ANA</u>, <u>anti-dsDNA</u>)

* Autoimmune reactions

* <u>Type III hypersensitivity</u> (most common in SLE) → <u>antibody-antigen complex</u> formation in <u>microvasculature</u> → <u>complement</u> activation and inflammation → damage to <u>skin</u>, <u>kidneys</u>, <u>joints</u>, small vessels

* <u>Type II hypersensitivity</u> → <u>IgG</u> and <u>IgM</u> <u>antibodies</u> directed against <u>antigens</u> on cells (e.g., <u>red blood cells</u>) → <u>cytopenia</u>

---

## Clinical features

SLE is a systemic disease characterized by phases of remission and relapse. Some individuals only experience mild symptoms, while others experience severe symptoms and rapid disease progression. SLE can affect any organ.




### Common [[6]](/library/KobU1u)




* Constitutional: : fatigue, <u>fever</u>, weight loss

* <u>Joints</u> (> 90% of cases) [[3]](/library/HMbKJ8)

* <u>Arthritis</u> and <u>arthralgia</u>

* <u>Distal</u> symmetrical <u>polyarthritis</u>: most commonly affects the <u>joints</u> of the fingers, carpal <u>joints</u>, and the knee

* <u>Skin</u> (85% of cases) [[3]](/library/HMbKJ8)[[7]](/library/inbJG8)

* Malar rash (<u>butterfly rash</u>): flat or raised fixed <u>erythema</u> over both malar eminences (<u>nasolabial folds</u> tend to be spared)

* <u>Raynaud phenomenon</u>

* <u>Photosensitivity</u> → <u>maculopapular rash</u>

* <u>Discoid rash</u>

* Oral <u>ulcers</u> (usually painless)

* Nonscarring <u>alopecia</u> (except with discoid rashes)

* <u>Periungual</u> <u>telangiectasia</u>





> [!TIP]
> Both <u>rheumatoid arthritis</u> and SLE <u>arthritis</u> affect the <u>MCP</u> and <u>PIP</u> <u>joints</u>, but SLE does not usually lead to deformities.

### Less common [[3]](/library/HMbKJ8)




* Hematological: : <u>petechiae</u>; , <u>pallor</u>, or recurrent infections due to <u>cytopenias</u>

* Musculoskeletal: <u>myalgia</u>

* <u>Serositis</u>: : <u>pleuritis</u> and <u>pericarditis</u> → effusions

* <u>Kidneys</u>: nephritis with <u>proteinuria</u> (see “<u>Lupus nephritis</u>”)

* <u>Heart</u>

* <u>Pericarditis</u>, <u>myocarditis</u>, <u>endocarditis</u> (<u>Libman-Sacks endocarditis</u>)

* <u>Aortic valve</u> lesions

* <u>Coronary artery disease</u>

* <u>Lungs</u>

* <u>Pneumonitis</u>

* <u>Interstitial lung disease</u>

* <u>Pulmonary hypertension</u>

* Vascular

* <u>Vasculitis</u>

* <u>Thromboembolism</u> (see “<u>Antiphospholipid syndrome</u>”)

* Neurological

* <u>Seizures</u>

* <u>Psychosis</u>

* <u>Personality</u> changes

* <u>Lupus cerebritis</u>

* <u>Aseptic meningitis</u>

* <u>Polyneuropathy</u>

* Eyes: <u>keratoconjunctivitis sicca</u>  [[8]](/library/EuY8GI)





> [!TIP]
> SLE can cause LSE (<u>Libman-Sacks</u> <u>Endocarditis</u>).

## Diagnosis

### General principles [[9]](/library/o3c0jX0)[[10]](/library/zRcrpX0)




* SLE is a <u>clinical diagnosis</u>.

* Consider a diagnosis of SLE in patients with <u>constitutional symptoms</u> and features involving ≥ 2 organs or systems.

* Rule out alternative diagnoses to avoid unnecessary and potentially harmful interventions (e.g., <u>immunosuppressants</u>).

* Diagnostic studies support the diagnosis and serve as markers of disease activity and/or organ damage.

* Rheumatology consultation is advised for all patients with suspected SLE.





> [!TIP]
> The <u>2019 EULAR/ACR classification criteria for SLE</u> may be considered to further support the diagnosis, but do not need to be fulfilled to establish a diagnosis of SLE. [[6]](/library/KobU1u)[[9]](/library/o3c0jX0)[[10]](/library/zRcrpX0)




> [!NOTE]
> “<u>SOAP</u> BRAIN, MD:” Serositis, Oral and/or nasal <u>ulcers</u>, Arthritis, Photosensitivity, Blood disorders, Renal involvement, ANAs, Immunological phenomena (<u>anti-dsDNA</u>, <u>anti-Sm</u>, <u>antiphospholipid antibodies</u>), Neurological disorders, and Malar or Discoid <u>rash</u> are the features of SLE.




### <u>Laboratory studies</u> [[9]](/library/o3c0jX0)[[10]](/library/zRcrpX0)




The following studies are commonly part of a minimum diagnostic workup if SLE is clinically suspected. [[9]](/library/o3c0jX0)




* <u>Antinuclear antibodies</u> (<u>ANAs</u>)

* Positive <u>titers</u> of ≥ 1:80 have ∼ 98% <u>sensitivity</u> for SLE (entry criterion for the <u>2019 EULAR/ACR classification criteria for SLE</u>).

* If negative, consider differential diagnoses and/or follow-up with the patient regularly.

* <u>Antigen-specific ANAs</u>: Request only if <u>ANAs</u> are positive.

* Anti-dsDNA antibodies

* <u>Autoantibodies</u> against double-stranded <u>DNA</u>

* Positive in 60–70% of patients

* Highly specific for SLE

* Levels correlate with disease activity (especially <u>lupus nephritis</u> activity).

* Anti-Sm antibodies

* <u>Autoantibodies</u> against Smith <u>antigens</u> (nonhistone nuclear <u>proteins</u>)

* Positive in < 30% of patients, but highly specific for SLE

* <u>Antiphospholipid antibodies</u>: Screen all patients for <u>antiphospholipid syndrome</u>.

* Laboratory markers of disease activity and/or organ damage in SLE

* <u>Complement</u> levels: ↓ C3 and/or ↓ C4 in patients with active disease

* <u>Inflammatory markers</u>  [[11]](/library/VicGqX0)

* <u>ESR</u>: may be elevated in patients with active disease

* <u>CRP</u>: often normal (may be elevated in patients with <u>serositis</u>, <u>arthritis</u>, or infections)

* <u>CBC</u>: may show <u>leukopenia</u>, <u>thrombocytopenia</u>, and/or <u>autoimmune hemolytic anemia</u> or <u>anemia of chronic disease</u>

* <u>CMP</u>: may show ↑ <u>BUN</u> and/or <u>creatinine</u>, and/or <u>electrolyte</u> abnormalities

* <u>Urinalysis</u> and urine microscopy: may show <u>proteinuria</u>; , <u>hematuria</u>, and/or <u>urinary casts</u>





> [!TIP]
> <u>ANAs</u> have the highest <u>sensitivity</u> but low <u>specificity</u> for SLE. <u>Anti-dsDNA</u> and <u>anti-Sm antibodies</u> are the most specific <u>antibodies</u> for SLE.




> [!NOTE]
> <u>RPR</u> and <u>VDRL</u> are usually used to <u>test for syphilis</u> but may also be positive in SLE.




![Red blood cell (RBC) casts in urine sediment](media/ua001ixegsnk5vrvnr6ft0hd.jpg)

Red blood cell (RBC) casts in urine sediment




### Classification criteria for SLE [[6]](/library/KobU1u)[[12]](/library/-RcDpX0)




The classification criteria for SLE were originally developed for research purposes (not as diagnostic criteria).  Nevertheless, these criteria are often used in clinical practice to support the diagnosis of SLE.




* Indication: Use in patients who have an <u>ANA</u> <u>titer</u> of ≥ 1:80;   (i.e., entry criterion;  for the classification criteria). [[6]](/library/KobU1u)

* Further considerations

* Consider other, more likely diagnoses before attributing a criterion to SLE.

* Criteria do not need to occur simultaneously.

* The occurrence of any criterion at least once is sufficient.

### Additional diagnostics [[9]](/library/o3c0jX0)




Request additional tests based on suspected organ involvement (see also “Specific clinical manifestations” and “Clinical features”).




#### Imaging studies




Imaging studies can help in the assessment of organ or <u>joint</u> involvement.




* <u>X-ray</u> <u>joints</u>: Perform in patients with articular symptoms.

* <u>X-ray</u> or CT chest: Perform in patients with symptoms of pulmonary involvement (e.g., <u>interstitial lung disease</u>, <u>pleuritis</u>).

* <u>Echocardiography</u>: Consider in patients with suspected <u>pericardial effusion</u> or <u>Libman-Sacks endocarditis</u>.





#### <u>Histopathology</u> [[13]](/library/hJbcFu)




* <u>Skin biopsy</u>

* Consider in patients with atypical dermatologic presentation or no response to initial therapy.

* Lupus band test (LBT): a <u>direct immunofluorescence</u> staining technique used to detect <u>immunoglobulin</u> and <u>complement component</u> deposits along the <u>dermoepidermal junction</u> in affected and unaffected <u>skin</u> in patients with SLE  [[14]](/library/jpb_6u)

* See also “<u>Cutaneous lupus erythematosus</u>.”

* <u>Kidney biopsy</u>: in case of suspected <u>lupus nephritis</u>





> [!TIP]
> <u>Biopsy</u> of an affected organ (e.g., <u>skin</u>, <u>kidney</u>) can be performed to support the diagnosis but is not required for all patients.




![Lupus band](media/ovau94pytuopyfoc9tvsh2ev.jpg)

Lupus band




#### <u>ASCVD risk assessment</u> [[9]](/library/o3c0jX0)




* Recommended in all patients with SLE (<u>ASCVD risk-enhancing factor</u>).   [[10]](/library/zRcrpX0)

* Includes <u>diabetes mellitus screening</u>, <u>screening for lipid disorders</u>, and a risk calculation using the <u>2013 ACC/AHA pooled cohort equation</u>





> [!TIP]
> Patients with SLE have double the cardiovascular risk compared to patients without SLE. Cardiovascular disease is among the most common <u>causes of death</u> in patients with SLE. [[10]](/library/zRcrpX0)

---

## Treatment

### General principles [[10]](/library/zRcrpX0)[[13]](/library/hJbcFu)[[15]](/library/0KYeUJ)




Specialist consultation is advised, i.e., rheumatology and other departments based on the patient's clinical presentation.




* Patients with SLE usually require life-long <u>immunosuppressants</u>. 

* Management is guided by disease severity and the systems or organs affected (see also “Specific clinical manifestations”).

* Patients should be frequently monitored for medication-induced adverse effects.

* <u>NSAIDs</u> can provide symptomatic relief.  [[9]](/library/o3c0jX0)

* Nonpharmacological measures include:

* <u>Lifestyle modifications for ASCVD prevention</u> (e.g., <u>smoking cessation</u>, aerobic exercise)

* Avoidance of <u>UV light</u>

* If applicable, optimize <u>management of ASCVD</u> and offer <u>preconception counseling</u> (see also “<u>SLE and pregnancy</u>”). [[10]](/library/zRcrpX0)





> [!WARNING]
> Admit patients with SLE and unexplained <u>fever</u>, severe disease (e.g., <u>lupus nephritis</u>, alveolar hemorrhage, <u>NPSLE</u>), or complications (e.g., <u>sepsis</u>, <u>thrombosis</u>), as these features are associated with increased mortality.




### Disease severity




Disease severity can be classified based on the presence of clinical features and <u>laboratory markers of disease activity and/or organ damage in SLE</u>.




* Mild disease (no vital organs affected): e.g., <u>constitutional symptoms</u>, mild <u>arthritis</u> <u>rash</u> and/or <u>cytopenias</u>

* Moderate disease (no vital organs affected): e.g., cutaneous <u>vasculitis</u>, <u>serositis</u>, <u>RA</u>-like <u>arthritis</u>, moderate <u>rash</u> and/or <u>cytopenias</u> , or no response to standard therapy

* Severe or organ-threatening disease: e.g., nephritis, <u>myelitis</u>, <u>pneumonitis</u>, <u>mesenteric</u> <u>vasculitis</u>, severe <u>cytopenias</u>





> [!TIP]
> Management should be guided by disease severity, the patient's safety (e.g., childbearing potential, adverse effects), and medication cost. Therapy may be modified further based on the main organs affected.




### Pharmacotherapy [[9]](/library/o3c0jX0)[[12]](/library/-RcDpX0)[[13]](/library/hJbcFu)




Depending on the systems or organs affected (e.g., <u>skin</u>, <u>kidneys</u>), a specialist may decide on a different pharmacological approach.




* All patients: <u>Hydroxychloroquine</u> is the cornerstone of therapy (regardless of disease activity).  [[13]](/library/hJbcFu)[[16]](/library/IicYGX0)

* Mild to moderate disease:  (no vital organs affected): Consider the addition of oral <u>glucocorticoids</u> with or without other <u>immunosuppressive agents</u> to achieve remission.

* Severe or organ-threatening disease

* <u>Induction therapy</u>

* High-dose IV <u>glucocorticoids</u> and other <u>immunosuppressive agents</u>

* Used until symptom remission or low disease activity is achieved

* <u>Maintenance of remission</u>

* <u>Hydroxychloroquine</u> with or without lower-dose <u>glucocorticoids</u>

* AND/OR <u>immunosuppressants</u> or <u>biological agents</u>

* Disease flares: Adjust therapy based on the severity of organ involvement.





| <br>Overview of the recommended pharmacological treatment for patients with non-renal SLE [[9]](/library/o3c0jX0)[[13]](/library/hJbcFu)<br> |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  |  | Disease severity |  |  |
|  |  | Mild to moderate | Severe |  |
| Standard therapy (for all patients) |  | <br>* <u>Hydroxychloroquine</u> DOSAGE [[13]](/library/hJbcFu)<br><br> |  |  |
| Additional therapy | <u>Glucocorticoids</u> | <br>* Low-dose, short-term, oral <u>glucocorticoids</u> (e.g., <u>prednisone</u> DOSAGE) [[13]](/library/hJbcFu)<br><br> |  | <br><br>* IV <u>glucocorticoids</u> (e.g., <u>methylprednisolone</u> DOSAGE) [[13]](/library/hJbcFu)<br><br>* Then initiate oral <u>prednisone</u> DOSAGE. [[13]](/library/hJbcFu)<br><br><br> |
| <br>Other <u>immunosuppressive agents</u> <br> | <br>* <u>Methotrexate</u> OR <u>azathioprine</u> (if there is no response to <u>hydroxychloroquine</u> plus low-dose <u>glucocorticoids</u>)<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Azathioprine</u>, <u>mycophenolate</u>, OR <u>cyclophosphamide</u><br><br>* <u>Biological agents</u><br><br>* E.g., <u>belimumab</u>, <u>rituximab</u>  [[13]](/library/hJbcFu)<br><br>* Indications: persistently active disease, frequent flares despite adequate treatment<br><br><br> |  |  |





#### Prevention and monitoring for medication-induced adverse effects [[9]](/library/o3c0jX0)[[10]](/library/zRcrpX0)[[13]](/library/hJbcFu)




* All patients: Offer <u>influenza</u> and <u>pneumococcus immunizations</u>.  [[9]](/library/o3c0jX0)

* <u>Glucocorticoids</u> and <u>immunosuppressants</u>

* Consider studies for the diagnosis of <u>latent TB</u> at baseline in selected patients.

* Assess for infection before starting high-dose <u>glucocorticoids</u>.

* Monitor for <u>side effects of glucocorticoid therapy</u>.

* <u>Hydroxychloroquine</u>: request ophthalmologic screening at baseline, after 5 years, and yearly thereafter.  [[13]](/library/hJbcFu)





> [!WARNING]
> Administer <u>glucocorticoids</u> at the lowest effective dose and only for short periods of time to reduce the risk of adverse effects (e.g., <u>hyperglycemia</u>, <u>atherosclerosis</u>, <u>myopathy</u>).




> [!TIP]
> Offer <u>vaccinations</u> before initiating pharmacological therapy based on the patient's individual risk and potential adverse effects of the prospective agent, and perform <u>laboratory studies</u>.

---

## Specific clinical manifestations

The specific manifestations of SLE are classified based on the systems affected.




### Cutaneous lupus erythematosus (CLE)




Some patients with lupus present with predominantly cutaneous manifestations. Cutaneous manifestations are classified based on their chronicity (acute, subacute, or chronic).




#### Acute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (<u>ACLE</u>) [[6]](/library/KobU1u)[[17]](/library/jLb_x8)[[18]](/library/oob01u)




* General information: frequently associated with active SLE

* <u>Epidemiology</u>: most common in individuals 20–30 years of age

* Clinical features

* <u>Malar rash</u>

* <u>Maculopapular rash</u> (also called <u>maculopapular rash</u> of lupus and photosensitive lupus dermatitis)

* Diagnostics

* Diagnosis is clinical.

* Consider a <u>biopsy</u> in patients with atypical clinical presentation.

* Serum studies

* Positive <u>ANAs</u> in 95% of patients [[17]](/library/jLb_x8)

* Levels of <u>anti-dsDNA</u> and <u>anti-Sm antibodies</u> are often positive.





> [!TIP]
> <u>ACLE</u> is frequently associated with systemic disease.




![Malar rash in systemic lupus erythematosus](media/pt1lsovai69lsk7ygp1akzuf.jpg)

Malar rash in systemic lupus erythematosus

![Malar rash](media/fggb1eluk24qrd3rathlmk61.jpg)

Malar rash

![Macular rash in systemic lupus erythematosus](media/bpfshe89pv3430s8h6ovbs4a.jpg)

Macular rash in systemic lupus erythematosus




#### Subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (<u>SCLE</u>) [[3]](/library/HMbKJ8)[[17]](/library/jLb_x8)




* General information

* An uncommon variant

* May be associated with systemic disease

* Clinical features

* Extreme <u>photosensitivity</u>

* Begins as a <u>papular</u> eruption or small scaly <u>plaques</u> that develop into either annular or <u>psoriasiform</u> lesions

* Lesions heal without scarring but may cause <u>hypopigmentation</u>.

* Usually affects the neck, shoulders, and upper limbs, but spares the face

* Diagnostics

* Based on a combination of <u>patient history</u>, <u>clinical examination</u>, and <u>histology</u>

* Patients often have positive <u>ANAs</u> and <u>anti-Ro/SSA antibodies</u>.





![Subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus](media/m5qrs3kr3tvcnag3p8xwwgcd.jpg)

Subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus

![Subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus](media/na32ixa9x9xidvirhlfa31ua.jpg)

Subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus




#### Discoid lupus erythematosus (<u>DLE</u>) [[7]](/library/inbJG8)[[17]](/library/jLb_x8)




* General information 

* Most common form of chronic CLE

* Rarely associated with systemic disease

* <u>Epidemiology</u>

* <u>♀</u> > <u>♂</u> (3:1)

* Most common in women 30–50 years of age

* Clinical features

* <u>Erythematous</u>, inflammatory scaly <u>plaques</u> that are painful to remove

* The <u>plaques</u> heal, but cause <u>scarring alopecia</u>, <u>atrophy</u>, peripheral <u>hyperpigmentation</u>, and central depigmentation.

* Typically affects the face, neck, and head (triggered by exposure to <u>UV light</u>)

* Diagnostics

* Based on a combination of <u>patient history</u> and <u>clinical examination</u>

* <u>Autoantibodies</u> ; (i.e., <u>ANAs</u> and <u>antigen-specific ANAs</u>) are usually negative.

* <u>Skin biopsy</u>: Consider in patients with atypical clinical presentation. [[13]](/library/hJbcFu)

* Vacuolar degeneration of <u>basal cells</u> (interface dermatitis) with <u>lymphocytic</u> infiltrates

* <u>Follicular hyperkeratosis</u> or plugging may be seen on the scalp and <u>mucin</u> deposition may be seen in long-standing lesions.

* <u>Lupus band test</u>: can help differentiate <u>DLE</u> from SLE  [[14]](/library/jpb_6u)

* Differential diagnosis: For details, see “<u>Overview of annular skin lesions</u>.”

* Prognosis

* The prognosis for patients with <u>DLE</u> is better than the prognosis for those with SLE.

* The risk of developing SLE is < 10%.





> [!TIP]
> <u>DLE</u> is the most common form of chronic CLE; it is rarely associated with systemic disease.

#### Management of CLE [[9]](/library/o3c0jX0)[[13]](/library/hJbcFu)




* General recommendations

* Wear sunblock with <u>SPF</u> ≥ 50 and protective clothing.

* See also “General principles” in the “Treatment” section.

* Pharmacological treatment (in consultation with a specialist)

* First-line treatment: <u>Hydroxychloroquine</u>

* PLUS topical <u>glucocorticoids</u> (e.g., <u>fluocinonide</u>) AND/OR topical <u>calcineurin inhibitors</u> (e.g., <u>pimecrolimus</u>) [[9]](/library/o3c0jX0)[[13]](/library/hJbcFu)

* With or without <u>systemic glucocorticoids</u> (e.g., <u>prednisone</u>)

* Second-line treatment (in consultation with a dermatologist) 

* Topical therapy: i.e., intralesional <u>steroids</u> for chronic <u>skin</u> lesions

* Systemic therapy: e.g., <u>methotrexate</u>, <u>retinoids</u>, <u>dapsone</u>, <u>thalidomide</u>, <u>belimumab</u>, or <u>rituximab</u>





### Lupus nephritis




#### Description [[19]](/library/hIYccq)




* Most dangerous specific manifestation because of its high <u>morbidity</u> and mortality

* Can manifest as <u>nephritic syndrome</u> and/or <u>nephrotic syndrome</u>; See also "<u>Nephritic-nephrotic syndrome</u>" in “<u>Glomerular diseases</u>."

* Common: found in up to 50% of individuals with SLE at presentation [[9]](/library/o3c0jX0)





#### Pathophysiology [[19]](/library/hIYccq)



* Mesangial and/or subendothelial deposition of <u>immune complexes</u> (e.g., <u>anti-dsDNA</u> <u>antibodies</u>, <u>anti-Sm</u> <u>antibodies</u>) → expansion and thickening of mesangium, <u>capillary</u> walls, and/or <u>glomerular basement membrane</u>




#### Clinical features




* <u>Hypertension</u>

* <u>Edema</u>

* <u>Hematuria</u>





#### Diagnostics [[9]](/library/o3c0jX0)




* <u>Laboratory studies</u>

* <u>BMP</u>: ↑ <u>creatinine</u>

* <u>Urinalysis</u>: <u>proteinuria</u>, <u>hematuria</u>, cellular casts (<u>RBCs</u>, <u>hemoglobin</u>, granular, tubular, or mixed)

* Spot <u>urine protein:creatinine ratio</u>: <u>proteinuria</u> ≥ 0.5 g/g

* <u>Kidney biopsy</u> 

* Indicated in patients with either: [[9]](/library/o3c0jX0)

* Unexplained ↑ <u>creatinine</u>

* <u>Proteinuria</u> ≥ 1.0 g/g

* <u>Proteinuria</u> ≥ 0.5 g/g and <u>hematuria</u> or cellular <u>urinary casts</u>

* Findings: <u>immune complex-mediated glomerulonephritis</u>





| <br>Abbreviated histopathologic classification of lupus nephritis  [[20]](/library/44c3jc0)<br> |  |
| --- | --- |
| Class I | <br>* Minimal mesangial disease<br><br> |
| Class II | <br>* Mesangial proliferative disease<br><br> |
| Class III | <br>* Focal <u>glomerular disease</u><br><br> |
| Class IV | <br>* Diffuse <u>glomerular disease</u>; can be further subdivided into:<br><br>* Segmental <u>glomerular disease</u> (Class IV-S)<br><br>* <u>Global</u> <u>glomerular disease</u> (Class IV-G)<br><br> |
| <br>Class V <br> | <br>* Membranous <u>glomerular disease</u><br><br> |
| Class VI | <br>* Advanced <u>sclerosing</u> disease<br><br> |





> [!TIP]
> Perform regular <u>urinalysis</u> follow-up in patients with SLE, as early detection and treatment of renal disease can prevent progression to severe disease.




![Red blood cell (RBC) casts in urine sediment](media/ua001ixegsnk5vrvnr6ft0hd.jpg)

Red blood cell (RBC) casts in urine sediment




#### Management of lupus nephritis [[13]](/library/hJbcFu)




* General principles

* Consult a nephrologist.

* Induction and <u>maintenance therapy</u> is generally indicated in patients with class III or IV <u>lupus nephritis</u>.

* All patients should receive standard therapy for lupus and individualized <u>management of CKD</u>.

* Pharmacological management

* <u>Induction therapy</u>

* IV <u>glucocorticoids</u> (e.g., <u>methylprednisolone</u>)

* PLUS other <u>immunosuppressants</u> (e.g., <u>mycophenolate</u> or <u>cyclophosphamide</u>)

* <u>Maintenance of remission</u>

* Oral <u>prednisone</u>

* PLUS <u>mycophenolate</u> OR <u>azathioprine</u>

* Refractory or relapsing disease: <u>Rituximab</u> may be considered.





> [!TIP]
> Patients with class I, II, or V <u>lupus nephritis</u> do not usually require specific <u>immunosuppressive therapy</u>. [[9]](/library/o3c0jX0)[[13]](/library/hJbcFu)




### Neuropsychiatric systemic lupus erythematosus (<u>NPSLE</u>) [[21]](/library/soXtW_)




* Description: the presence of neurological and psychiatric symptoms in patients with SLE that cannot be attributed to another condition [[22]](/library/1KY22J)

* <u>Epidemiology</u>: found in ∼ 40% of patients with SLE [[21]](/library/soXtW_)

* Classification: The American College of Rheumatology has identified 19 <u>NPSLE</u> syndromes. [[22]](/library/1KY22J)





| <br><u>Neuropsychiatric systemic lupus erythematosus</u> syndromes [[22]](/library/1KY22J)<br> |  |
| --- | --- |
| <u>Central nervous system</u> | <u>Peripheral nervous system</u> |
| <br><br>* <u>Aseptic meningitis</u><br><br>* <u>Cerebrovascular disease</u><br><br>* <u>Demyelination</u><br><br>* <u>Headache</u><br><br>* <u>Chorea</u><br><br>* <u>Myelopathy</u><br><br>* <u>Seizures</u><br><br>* Acute confusional state<br><br>* <u>Anxiety disorder</u><br><br>* Cognitive impairment<br><br>* <u>Mood disorder</u><br><br>* <u>Psychosis</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy</u> (<u>Guillain-Barré syndrome</u>)<br><br>* Autonomic disorder<br><br>* Single mononeuropathy or <u>mononeuropathy multiplex</u><br><br>* <u>Myasthenia gravis</u><br><br>* <u>Cranial neuropathy</u><br><br>* <u>Plexopathy</u><br><br>* <u>Polyneuropathy</u><br><br><br> |





* Diagnostics  [[21]](/library/soXtW_)

* General principles

* Rule out other common etiologies (e.g., infections, <u>malignancy</u>, adverse drug effects).

* Consult a <u>neurologist</u> if <u>NPSLE</u> is suspected.

* Imaging studies

* First-line studies: <u>MRI</u> <u>brain</u> (T1/<u>T2-weighted</u>) may detect <u>NPSLE</u> and also rule out other neurosurgical lesions and infections.

* Consider other studies (e.g., <u>EEG</u>, <u>SPECT</u>) depending on clinical features.

* <u>Laboratory studies</u>

* <u>CSF</u> examination: Request for patients with a suspected neurological infection.

* <u>Serology</u>: <u>antiphospholipid antibodies</u>, <u>ANAs</u>

* See also the “Diagnostics” section.

* Treatment: depends on the underlying cause [[21]](/library/soXtW_)

* Antithrombotic and/or <u>antiplatelet therapy</u> for <u>ischemic</u>, embolic, or <u>thrombotic</u> manifestations

* <u>Immunosuppressive treatment</u> for inflammatory manifestations: See also the “Treatment” section.

---

## Differential diagnoses

### Drug-induced lupus erythematosus (<u>DILE</u>) [[9]](/library/o3c0jX0)[[23]](/library/9LbN-8)




* Description: : lupus-like symptoms triggered by medication

* <u>Epidemiology</u>

* <u>♂</u> = <u>♀</u>

* <u>DILE</u> accounts for ∼ 10% of all SLE cases.

* Most common in white populations

* Most common in individuals 50–70 years of age

* Etiology

* Genetic susceptibility

* Presence of a genetic mutation that causes decreased acetyltransferase activity, which results in the slow <u>acetylation</u> of drugs

* Presence of <u>HLA-DR2</u>, <u>HLA-DR3</u>, <u>HLA-DR4</u>, or an unexpressed C4 <u>complement</u> <u>allele</u>

* Drug triggers [[23]](/library/9LbN-8)

* High risk: <u>procainamide</u> and <u>hydralazine</u>

* Low risk: <u>sulfa drugs</u>;  and certain nonsulfa drugs, (e.g., <u>isoniazid</u>, <u>methyldopa</u>, <u>minocycline</u>, <u>phenytoin</u>, <u>TNF-α inhibitors</u>)

* Clinical features (usually manifest ≥ 1 month after medication initiation)

* Constitutional: fatigue, <u>fever</u>, and weight loss

* Musculoskeletal: <u>myalgia</u> and symmetrical <u>polyarthralgia</u>

* <u>Skin</u> lesions (e.g., <u>malar rash</u>)

* <u>Serositis</u>

* Diagnostics [[9]](/library/o3c0jX0)[[23]](/library/9LbN-8)

* <u>ANAs</u> are positive in nearly all patients.

* Antihistone antibodies

* Antihistone <u>antibodies</u> are seen in 90–95% of patients.

* Nonspecific: They may also be present in ∼ 75% of patients with SLE.

* <u>Anti-dsDNA antibodies</u>: uncommon in patients with <u>DILE</u>

* Treatment

* Stop the triggering drug.

* If necessary, start temporary pharmacotherapy (see the “Treatment” section).

* Prognosis: Most cases resolve within a few weeks after the causative medication has been discontinued.





> [!NOTE]
> “My Two HIPS”: Methyldopa/Minocycline, TNF-α inhibitors, Hydralazine, Isoniazid, Procainamide/Phenytoin, and Sulfa drugs are triggers for <u>DILE</u>.




> [!TIP]
> <u>DILE</u> can manifest with various features that are also seen in <u>idiopathic</u> SLE (e.g., <u>fever</u>, <u>arthritis</u>, <u>malar rash</u>, <u>serositis</u>) but typically does not affect the <u>CNS</u> or <u>kidneys</u>, unlike SLE.




### Undifferentiated connective tissue disease (<u>UCTD</u>)




* Definition: a term used to describe a clinical entity that manifests with features of <u>autoimmunity</u> without fulfilling the criteria for any specific <u>connective tissue disease</u>

* Classification criteria [[24]](/library/KQcUCX0)

* Clinical features that suggest a systemic autoimmune disease

* Positive <u>ANAs</u> on two separate occasions

* Disease duration of ≥ 3 years

* Approach to management [[24]](/library/KQcUCX0)

* Provide the patient with clear information on the diagnosis.

* Refer to a rheumatologist for periodical follow-up.

* No specific therapy is required; consider symptomatic management.

* Prognosis: Up to 25% of patients with <u>UCTD</u> progress to an identifiable systemic autoimmune disease within 1–3 years. [[24]](/library/KQcUCX0)





> [!TIP]
> In patients with <u>UCTD</u>, the presence of <u>serositis</u>, <u>fever</u>, and/or <u>anti-Sm</u> or <u>anti-dsDNA antibodies</u> has been associated with progression to SLE. [[25]](/library/V-aGwM)




The differential diagnoses listed here are not exhaustive.

---

## Special patient groups

### SLE and pregnancy




* General [[26]](/library/jOY_H6)[[27]](/library/POYWs6)

* While <u>fertility</u> is not affected by SLE, it may be affected by <u>immunosuppressive drugs</u>.

* <u>Pregnancy</u> may trigger flares in disease activity.

* Increased severity of maternal disease correlates with increased risk of maternal and fetal complications during <u>pregnancy</u> (see “Complications” below).

* Risk assessment [[26]](/library/jOY_H6)[[27]](/library/POYWs6)

* Cardiac, <u>lung</u>, and <u>kidney</u> screening  [[27]](/library/POYWs6)

* Serological profile

* <u>Anti-Ro/SSA</u> and <u>anti-La/SSB</u> are associated with an increased risk of <u>neonatal lupus</u>.

* <u>Anticardiolipin antibodies</u> and <u>lupus anticoagulant</u>: ↑ risk of <u>miscarriage</u> and <u>thrombosis</u>-related complications (see “<u>Antiphospholipid syndrome</u>”)

* Management [[15]](/library/0KYeUJ)[[27]](/library/POYWs6)

* <u>Pregnancy planning</u> and counseling  [[26]](/library/jOY_H6)

* Medical treatment should not be discontinued but the drug regimen may be changed. 

* Preconception, <u>pregnancy</u>, and <u>breastfeeding</u>: <u>hydroxychloroquine</u> and/or <u>azathioprine</u>

* Disease flares: <u>hydroxychloroquine</u> and/or <u>prednisolone</u>

* Low-dose <u>aspirin</u> from 12 weeks' <u>gestation</u> reduces the risk of <u>preeclampsia</u>. [[27]](/library/POYWs6)

* <u>Teratogenic</u> <u>immunosuppressive drugs</u> (e.g., <u>methotrexate</u>, <u>mycophenolate</u>, <u>cyclophosphamide</u>) should be avoided.

* Complications [[27]](/library/POYWs6)

* Maternal

* SLE flares

* <u>Hypertension</u>, <u>preeclampsia</u>

* <u>Venous thromboembolism</u>

* Fetal-neonatal

* <u>Neonatal lupus syndrome</u>

* <u>Miscarriage</u>

* <u>Intrauterine growth restriction</u>

* Fetal <u>AV block</u>  [[26]](/library/jOY_H6)

* <u>Preterm delivery</u>





> [!WARNING]
> Avoid <u>estrogen</u>-containing <u>hormonal contraceptives</u> in patients with <u>antiphospholipid syndrome</u> because of the increased risk of <u>thrombosis</u>.




> [!TIP]
> Educate patients of reproductive age about <u>contraceptive</u> methods, planned <u>pregnancy</u>, and the potential <u>teratogenic</u> effects of pharmacological treatment.




### Neonatal lupus syndrome [[26]](/library/jOY_H6)[[27]](/library/POYWs6)




* General: rare (has a high <u>mortality rate</u>)

* Etiology: associated with the transfer of maternal <u>antibodies</u> (<u>anti-Ro/SSA</u> and <u>anti-La/SSB</u>)

* Clinical features

* First- to third-degree congenital <u>AV block</u>

* Periorbital or diffuse <u>rash</u> (often presents in the first weeks after <u>birth</u>)

* <u>Cytopenia</u>

* <u>Hepatitis</u>, <u>elevated liver enzymes</u>

* Diagnostics
* The following two criteria must be present at <u>birth</u>:

* <u>Antibodies</u> (<u>anti-Ro/SSA</u> or <u>anti-La/SSB</u>) in either the mother or child

* <u>Heart block</u>, characteristic <u>rash</u>, and/or hematologic/hepatic involvement with no identifiable cause in the <u>newborn</u>/fetus

* Treatment: directed at specific organ involvement

* Prognosis: Symptoms usually resolve within a few months.





![Neonatal lupus syndrome](media/geqtdirfmcnxvejgfuf2f6h0.jpg)

Neonatal lupus syndrome

---

## Complications

### Infections [[13]](/library/hJbcFu)[[28]](/library/Cqbq0E)




* Responsible for 25–50% of deaths in patients with SLE  [[28]](/library/Cqbq0E)

* Most common infections

* Bacterial: <u>skin</u>, <u>lungs</u>, and <u>urinary tract</u>

* Viral: varicella zoster <u>virus</u>, <u>cytomegalovirus</u>, and <u>human papillomavirus</u>





> [!TIP]
> Patients with SLE are at increased risk of developing infections because of disease-related factors (e.g., <u>pancytopenia</u>) and/or <u>immunosuppressive treatment</u>.




### Cardiovascular disease [[15]](/library/0KYeUJ)




* ↑ Risk of <u>thrombosis</u>;  in all patients with SLE (especially if secondary <u>antiphospholipid syndrome</u> is present)

* ↑ Risk of <u>myocardial infarction</u> and <u>stroke</u> because of accelerated <u>atherosclerosis</u>





### Other comorbidities [[3]](/library/HMbKJ8)[[29]](/library/Epb8ru)




* <u>Libman-Sacks endocarditis</u>

* <u>Pancytopenia</u>

* <u>Non-Hodgkin lymphoma</u> [[30]](/library/dzco7U0)

* <u>Osteonecrosis</u> of long-bone <u>epiphyses</u> (e.g., <u>osteonecrosis of the femoral head</u>) [[31]](/library/sRWtoO0)

* <u>Interstitial lung disease</u>, <u>pulmonary hypertension</u>

* Medication-induced adverse effects

* <u>Pregnancy</u>-related adverse effects (see “<u>SLE and pregnancy</u>” in “Special patient groups” below)





We list the most important complications. The selection is not exhaustive.

---

## Prognosis

* Mortality: 10-year survival rate is ∼ 90% [[3]](/library/HMbKJ8)[[29]](/library/Epb8ru)

* <u>Causes of death</u> [[3]](/library/HMbKJ8)

* In early disease

* High disease activity with renal or neurological complications

* Infections due to disease-related factors and <u>immunosuppressive therapy</u>

* In late disease

* Cardiovascular disease [[29]](/library/Epb8ru)

* Complications due to <u>atherosclerosis</u>

* <u>Coronary artery disease</u>

* Most common <u>cause of death</u> in SLE [[32]](/library/IkbY6F)

* <u>End-stage renal disease</u>  [[19]](/library/hIYccq)

* Adverse effects of long-term medication





> [!NOTE]
> “Redness In Cheeks” (<u>malar rash</u>): Renal disease, Infections, and Cardiovascular complications are the three most common <u>causes of death</u> in SLE.




> [!TIP]
> Damage to the <u>kidneys</u> or nervous system is associated with a poor prognosis.

---
